2. The plaintiff-petitioner instituted the aforesaid suit for declaration and permanent injunction upon the averments that the petitioner as the mutwalli of two waqf estates created by his great grandfather late Chowdhury Raisuddin Ahmed Siddiky and his grand-father late Khan Bahadur Kasemuddin Ahmed Siddiky unsuccessfully challenged by Writ Petition No. 80 of 1957 the general Notification, Nos. 4836-L.R. and 4849-L.R. both dated 2.4.56 purporting to acquire en block with effect from 14.4.56 all the remaining rent-receiving interest in the District of Dhaka under section 3(1) and all khas lands under section 3(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Thereafter on 24.5.60 Ordinance No. IX of 1960 was promulgated amending the said Act by adding a new section l0A and on 7.2.62 Ordinance No.IV of 1962 was promulgated providing, inter alia, that the then Provincial Government having not exercised the right of possession in respect of waqf and debuttor interests after the aforesaid notification, the mutwalli or shebait shall continue and be deemed to have continued to manage such interests as the agent of the then Provincial Government till the last day of the agricultural year next following the date of publication of the notification under section 43(2) of the Act declaring that Compensation Assessment Roll in respect of such interest has been finally published. It is the plaintiffs contention that the Compensation Assessment Roll in respect of the two waqf estates in question have not been prepared in accordance with the terms of the said Act and the rules framed thereunder. The plaintiff has given particulars of non-compliance of the Act and the rules. He stated that he was still in undisturbed and unhampered possession of all the properties of the concerned waqf estates as mutwalli even after the aforesaid general notification by realising rents and tolls, except the forest lands described in schedule -III of the plaint. When the plaintiffs possession was threatened by the officers of the defendant No.1, the then Province of East Pakistan, the plaintiff again filed Writ Petition No.146 of 1964, but a Special Bench of the High Court of East Pakistan discharged the Rule on 7.4.65 by a majority decision holding that the plaintiffs waqf estates stood acquired under the notifications dated 2.4.56. The plaintiff preferred Civil Appeal No. 27-D of 1965 in the then Supreme Court of Pakistan and obtained an order of stay on 15.8.65. The appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court of Pakistan on 26.2.68 with the observation, inter alia, that if there be any defect in the proceedings which culminated in the publication of the Compensation Assessment Rolls, then it would still be open to the plaintiff-petitioner to agitate the matter in the proper forum. Upon these averments the plaintiffs prayer No.1 in the suit was as follows:- 

 "(i) For a declaration that no valid Compensation Assessment Roll in respect of the properties in suit has been prepared and finally published within the meaning of section 43 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, and the plaintiffs right to possess and manage the said properties has not been affected by the publication of the alleged Compensation Assessment Roll as claimed by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2." 

 "2. Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, on the commencement of this Order, all suits, appeals, applications and other legal proceedings pending or continuing or deemed to be pending or continuing in any Court against the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh in which the legality or validity of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (E.B. Act No. XXVIII of 1951), or of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 (E.B. Ord. No. III of 1956), or of any other law making any amendment in the said Act, or of the acquisition of any property made under any provision thereof is challenged or called in question shall abate, and all orders, including orders of injunction and other interlocutory orders, passed in such suits, appeals, applications and other legal proceedings shall cease to have any effect and no court shall entertain), and no person shall bring any fresh suit,appeal, application or other legal proceeding's in which the legality or validity of any such law or acquisition is challenged or called in question." 

 17. I find that Article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972 starts with a non-obstante clause, namely, "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force". President's Order No. 69 of 1972 came into force on 16.6.72 and President's Order No. 90 of 1972 came into force 003.8.72 . It seems to be very clear that Article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972 also refers to Article 4(1) of President's Order No. 69 of 1972 by mentioning suits etc. "deemed to be pending or continuing in any Court against the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh". Needless to say, suits etc. were "deemed to be pending or continuing in any Court against the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh" only by virtue of Article 4 (1) of President's Order No. 69 of 1972. Therefore, Article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972 obviously makes a new provision of abatement in regard to some particular suits. It is well-established that when a non-obstante clause is used it has first to be ascertained what the enacting part of the section provides on a fair construction of words used according to their natural and ordinary meaning and the non obstante clause is to be understood as operating to set aside as no longer valid anything contained in relevant existing law which is inconsistent with the new enactment. The plain meaning of Article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972 is that suits in which the legality or validity of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 or of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 or of any other law making any amendment in the said Act or to the acquisition of any property made under any provision thereof is challenged or called in question shall abate. Suits answering this description, therefore, fall under a second category of automatic abatement and it is neither necessary for or open to the Government to prefer an application under Article 4(2) of President's Order No. 69 of 1972 to opt out of suits of such nature. President's Order No. 69 of 1972 and President's Order No. 90 of 1972 are mutually exclusive in respect of suits of the above description. 

 21. But Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed has submitted that the suit can legitimately be severed, in that the plaintiff has neither challenged the legality and validity of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 or of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 or of any other law making any amendment in the said Act, or of the acquisition of any property made under any provision thereof, when the plaintiff-petitioner averred that the Compensation Assessment Roll was not prepared in terms of the Act and the rules and that he is entitled, therefore, to possess and manage the waqf properties till the Compensation Assessment Roll is validly prepared, because that is a right given to him under section 10A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. 

 22. The substance of Mr. Ahmed's contention is that the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 having been amended by incorporation of a new section 10A by Ordinance No. IX of 1960, whereby possession of a waqf property which has been acquired under section 3(1) and 3(2) of the Act by its mutwali has been protected till after the final publication of the Compensation Assessment Roll, the plaintiff-petitioner has a right under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act itself to agitate that there has not been a valid Compensation Assessment Roll lawfully prepared and that there has not been a lawful final publication thereof within the meaning of section 42. Therefore, any notification purported to be issued under sub-section (2) of section 43 declaring such publication of the Compensation Assessment Roll is a nullity and of no legal effect. The Government does not acquire in that view of the matter any right to take over possession of the waqf property from the mutwalli who is deemed to be in possession of the waqf properties as an agent of the Government. Mr. Ahmed contends that in order to en-force the mutwalli's right of existing possession as against the Government in terms of section 10A of the Act, he need not challenge the legality or validity of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 or the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 or the acquisition of the aforesaid property under any provision thereof. Therefore, he submits that the question of abatement of the suit under the provision of President's Order No. 90 of 1972 does not arise so far as the first prayer for decree, as stated in the plaint, is concerned. 

 25. I have carefully considered the decision reported in 33 DLR (AD) 13 and have compared the facts of the case with the present case. In the aforecited case the plaintiff-respondent very clearly wanted to challenge the very acquisition of the debuttor property by notices of wholesale acquisition. This challenge came within the mischief of Article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972. The further prayer for a declaration that no Compensation Assessment Roll with regard to the plaintiff debuttor estate have been prepared or published in terms of the Act and rules thereunder does appear to be a consequential prayer flowing from the main prayer, because there is no averment and no prayer that the plaintiff-respondent wants to protect his possession till the Compensation Assessment Roll is lawfully prepared and published. In the present suit, however, the plaintiff has candidly stated that all his efforts to declare the general notification of wholesale acquisition to be null and void has ended in failure, but he now wants to protect his possession under the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 itself till the Compensation Assessment Roll is lawfully prepared and published. Rather it appears to, me that he challenges the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 in a speculative manner, devised as an after-thought, formulated upon a chance information. This challenge does not appear to me to be the main burden of the plaintiffs suit. The suit can well proceed without this challenge. Therefore, I am of the opinion that the whole suit does not abate. It is only the plaintiffs averments in paragraphs 14-16 of the plaint and his prayer No. (ii) which abate in the facts, and circumstances of the case.
